Oct`2007 to Dec’2007  JOB TITLE Software Developer  
JOB DESCRIPTION
Firmware Developer responsible for 
Sustaining and enhancing ESB2 server management firmware stack.
Design and implement client side utility to configure and monitor the server management firmware stack.

KEY ACCOMPLISHMENTS
ESB2 FW Sustaining:
Jason joined the team at the beginning of Q4 `07. During that quarter he made significant contribution to make the team meet important milestones. He effectively leveraged his prior work experience with the group as an intern. He started attending escalation meetings from day one. Early on, Jason helped to reproduce and characterize critical customer issue on Fox Cove, which laid the groundwork for a timely resolution of the problem. Jason’s expertise in network came in handy to recreate a problem reported by a key customer. The network setup that he put in place was used to debug and provide a confident fix for this issue.

IPDC Transport Library:
Jason was assigned to work on transport library for the DCMI conformance suite. He collaborated with senior engineers in releasing the first cut of transport library. He coordinated with Poland team to define generic transport APIs for use by applications. In a short time, he was able to provide working code of high quality.

Strengths
Risk Taking:
When Jason is presented with a problem, he asks for time to understand it and often comes up with more than one way to solve it. Jason never shies away from issues, because it is new to him, he makes an effort to learn as much as much as he can and diligently works towards establishing a baseline of knowledge to start from.

Result Orientation:
Maintains a clear vision of what is required and demonstrates the drive and determination to achieve results. Jason is able to work with minimal supervision. 

AREAS FOR IMPROVEMENT/DEVELOPMENT
Software Methodology: 
As part of his software career development, Jason should become well versed in processes and methodologies, and make it a part of his working style. He should get into a mode of organizing design and code review with his peers; work with validation to make sure the test plan provides good code overage etc…

Broaden Technical Expertise: 
The ESB2 SDK firmware is a good learning vehicle to understand basic concepts in real time programming. He should take advantage of the wealth of knowledge within the team to pick up some tips and tricks of embedded system programming and advanced debugging techniques. He should also plan on attending course to help him gain exposure to internal processor and chipset architecture.

Status Update:
Jason should provide status updates on the projects he is working on without being asked. He should summarize where he is on the problem he is assigned to work on and not leave the stake holders guessing. Periodical email updates is highly recommended.

PERFORMANCE SUMMARY
Jason is an asset to the firmware development team. Though he was with the team for only one quarter in 2007, he has established himself as a significant contributor. He is fast and efficient in coming up with solutions. 

Jason has been rated successful for 2008 focal. Thanks for your hard work Jason!

focal_gems.full_text:
Review Period January 2008 - December 2008  Job Title Firmware Developer Grade 5  
Job Description
During this review period, Jason worked as a firmware developer in the CCG SSE group for ESB2 and Willowbrook DCMI development.

Key Accomplishments/Deliverables

DCMI & DCTS
In this Focal cycle, Jason worked on the network/API portion of the DCMI Conformance Test Suite.  He continued to support DCTS and carried his experience on to two other projects (Red Dog and SOL API).  The work on DCTS transports uncovered several cipher suite bugs in Bensley and Thurley implementations.  Jason worked with his peers and successfully debugged and published the solutions.
The Red Dog project involved porting the DCTS network transport and was expected to be used by Microsoft. Jason quickly provided a proof of concept and later demonstrated the product to Microsoft.  Jason teamed up with another senior team member to develop a SOL API solution capable of replacing the serial IP dongles used by the Microsoft data center. The project served as a way to become familiar with and explore the SOL protocol and a full product life cycle.  
Jason gained a depth understanding of SOL protocol, general API requirements, threading, data flow, and memory allocation.  He demonstrated such skills as teamwork, brainstorming, design, documentation, and validation as part of this project.  The end result was a software package owned by SSE that provided an alternative to other open & closed source SOL clients.

Willowbrook Development
Implementing the "Get Asset tag" DCMI command was Jason's first opportunity to add a new feature to iBMC firmware.  This implementation involved the creation of a full document process which was followed with research, design, CCB, implementation, and code review.  During the Willowbrook DCMI development, he also actively drove and participated in code reviews for the DCMI/IPMI stack type, command handler, and DHCP features.  Using his familiarity with the team’s work, Jason was able to do an emergency manual merge against the latest EPSD code base, allowing the team to meet the deadline. He also worked on several trackers with root causing efforts and fixed several cipher related issues.

Evaluation: Strengths

Quality & Problem solving
When Jason was challenged to learn areas outside of his comfort zone, he met each opportunity with enthusiasm. He continuously challenged himself to learn new areas including socket network programming, threading, and embedded Linux debugging.  He used many brainstorming sessions early in the development phase of the SOL API to continuously strive to refine its design.  Later, the design proved flexible enough to be able to drastically change the API due to issues exposed by validation.  SSE lead architect Hari Ramachandran publicly recognized the quality and speed with which the project had been worked and compared it favorably with an earlier effort from a larger team.  The DCMI Asset tag was a similar success. After completion, only one bug was found which uncovered a design flaw in a larger scope.

Jason has positive problem solving skills, and has demonstrated this in the way he approaches all problems. He came up with creative solutions to a problem and delivers it with good quality. He unit tests his code and asks for help when necessary. He has demonstrated this in all his deliveries. These qualities have rendered him to take on complex trackers.

Great Place to work & Results Orientation
Jason has been recognized as an excellent team player and goes beyond his capacity to help others. He is open, direct and honest in his communication. He brings forth good points to discussion and grasps concepts rather quickly. This skill allowed Jason to shape solutions that were easy for his customers to comprehend. For example, the build process that Jason created was appreciated by all team members as being simple and easy to understand. He also helped the validation team with FTF smoke test framework and fixing Aardvark I2C issues.

Jason used his results orientation skills when supporting customer requests by quickly working critical issues and unexpected immediate requests with good spirits and made on-time delivery. Some examples include, writing an ipmitool power cycle script for reliability testing, creating a shell script to provision the BMC's LAN interface in Linux for Yahoo, converting the 'ipmitool dcmi' patch to a script for release to DCMI customers, finding a method to simulate an "ARP storm" for validation and helped with "DCMI only" effort during early DCMI Willowbrook development.


AREAS FOR IMPROVEMENT/DEVELOPMENT

Discipline: Jason has missed a few delivery dates and meetings.  At times, he loses direction on tasks. Jason is always willing to help other team members, which is good, but that should not be at the cost of his own tasks and deliverables. He should maintain a fine balance between his deliverables and helping others. He needs to set priorities for himself, and make sure he commits to his schedule and escalate quickly if he thinks he is not able to progress further. More recently, Jason has exhibited productive discipline by regularly attending the meetings and inputting the status of his tasks. He should continue this trend and assume his tasks responsibility and meet the commitments in an uncompromising fashion. 


Written/Verbal Communication: 
Jason’s emails and documentation appear cryptic; the contents are hard to understand. It is critical
to set the right context and give clarity in emails those are distributed to teams internal and 
external; this is also critical with technical documentation. As email communication has become a 
very necessary tool for work at Intel, Jason needs make sure of spending right amount of time in
articulating the emails and can use the approach of getting it reviewed with a buddy or team lead before publishing. The same approach can be used with technical documentation as well. 



PERFORMANCE SUMMARY   

Jason has been rated Successful for focal 2009. Thanks for your contributions Jason!

focal_gems.full_text:
Review Period January 2009 - December 2009  Job Title Firmware Engineer Grade 5  
Job Description
Jason was a firmware developer in the CCG SSE group in 2009 for Willowbrook and Westerlee DCMI development.


Key Accomplishments
Willowbrook
Jason delivered the Serial over LAN (SOL) performance tool in partnership with another team member. This tool enabled the team in SSE to validate and quantify SOL manageability feature performance on Willowbrook. The team was able to reuse existing SOL library to accelerate the tool availability for Willowbrook SOL validation.   

Jason added multi session support to DCTS conformance test suite libraries, this helped Intel to release DCTS with multi session support as part of DCMI 1.0 errata update release.

Jason piloted and used the validation smoke test suite for Willowbrook developer testing. This enabled the firmware development team to smoke test their code after proceeding into the build.

Westerlee
Jason participated in early Westerlee FAS design brain storming sessions with the DM system architect, providing input to initial designs. One of his key inputs was pointing out the weakness of reused packets in the command handler; this later turned out as a core concept for IPMI stack design.

Jason was part of a three member team that delivered the low level design for serial over lan (SOL). His prior SOL expertise was a plus in brainstorming sessions. Jason’s counter-proposal to the original SOL design was a winner due to its simplicity. As part of this team, he quickly ramped up on the existing ME Kernel HECI driver and worked closely with his team members to finalize the low level design of DCMI over HECI (DoH). He completed the implementation of the DoH module as well. This provided the developer and validation teams an interface to talk to ME Westerlee DM firmware.

Jason also delivered low level designs for system event log (SEL) and platform configuration control (PCC) components. During the implementation of PCC, Jason reviewed dependent component designs and identified gaps with IPMI message packet length and platform database API usage. He drove design owners to address these gaps.


Evaluation: Strengths
Process
Jason paid close attention to the development process for areas of improvement.  He helped in evaluating a code review tool that helped the team adopt a faster code review process.  Jason became familiar with the SCRUM methodology and actively participated in monthly feedback meetings. This allowed the team to continuously improve and strengthen the agile process.  As a result of his focus on SCRUM Jason improved on setting goals and time estimation.

Problem solving
Jason focused on “doing the right things right”.  He often challenged the design, code and process areas that had potential problems. He escalated the issues to the right owner to resolve the problem. 
Jason has good problem solving skills, and he demonstrated this in the way he approached all problems. He initiated creative solutions to problems and drove them to successful completion. 
Technical skills
This year was Jason’s first opportunity as a firmware developer to contribute early in the design process.  He was able to learn how to write technical documentation and code from scratch by addressing the team’s review feedback effectively. 


Evaluation: Areas for Development and/or Improvement
Discipline: 
At times, Jason loses direction on his tasks. Jason is always willing to help other team members, which is good, but that should not be at the cost of his own tasks and deliverables. He should maintain a balance between his commitments and helping others. He needs to set priorities for himself, and ensure he commits to his schedule and escalate quickly. This would include seeking assistance from senior developers, if he is not able to progress further. More recently, Jason has exhibited better discipline by regularly updating the scrum website and inputting the status of his tasks in scrum meetings. He should continue this trend by taking ownership of his tasks and meeting commitments in an uncompromising fashion. 

Written Communication: 
Jason has shown improvement in his written communication last year through low level design documents, but there is significant room for improvement. Jason should clearly communicate his intentions and expectations to his stake holders.  There have been times when Jason sent out an email in a cryptic form that made it difficult for other team members to understand. It is critical to set the right context and give clarity in emails that are distributed to the team. This is equally important in technical documentation. Jason should ensure that he is articulating his point clearly in technical documentation and emails. He should consider the approach of getting it reviewed with a buddy or team lead before publishing. 

Quality:
Jason should improve the quality of his code and try to understand the complete requirements of the assigned module. As DOH (DCMI over Heci) module was his first firmware module to be designed and developed from scratch, Jason quickly created the initial implementation of DoH. But he did not understand the complete requirements and did not bring it to the appropriate quality level.  Whether he is working on a new module development or bug fixing, he should understand the development process and follow the necessary guidelines of firmware development every time.

Performance Summary

Jason has been rated Successful for focal 2010. Thanks for your contributions Jason!


Job Title Firmware Engineer Grade 5
Job Description
o Jason was a Firmware Engineer working in the PCG/SSE FW team, and was responsible for
delivering server manageability solutions for Intel Server chipsets in 2010.
Key Accomplishments
o Process, Build, BVT & Lab support: Jason supported numerous builds, BVT, NTE and Lab
issues; expediting resolution of the problems. Jason provided back-up coverage for the primary
build engineer and demonstrated technical competence in understanding the build system.
Within the complex and shared build infrastructure, Jason identified potential issues and worked
with the team to address them. He also supported BVT and the NTE activities for the team by
providing technical assistance in debugging various problems. His efforts in this area helped the
team meet overall Westerlee project milestones.
Jason was a key resource for general lab, KVM and networking issues. He helped define new
hosts requirements, OS image, and took responsibility for adding new hosts to the domain.
Jason supported the DHCP severs in both the validation and development labs. Jason also
participated in scrum process improvement discussions, and was enthusiastic about incorporating
improvements.
o Firmware Development
Jason was assigned defects related to the LAN implementation and he investigated several that
appeared to involve the RAKP protocol. Jason’s ability to understand RAKP+ and RMCP+
protocols, FTF and Xtrans empowered him to resolve the defects. Jason also investigated
problems in SOL and Linux, where he found a configuration that allowed this important
functionality to be available for the product. While working defects assigned to him, Jason was
able to identify other bugs in the process. Jason investigated the initial failure of the firmware
with DCTS 1.0 and worked with the architect to develop a solution. Jason ran further tests and
enabled another engineer to complete the task of making the necessary changes for the
firmware to pass DCTS.
Evaluation: Strengths
o Technical Expertise: Jason has diverse technical skills that were of significant value to the
team. His experience with validation tools and scripts was a plus, and his knowledge of RAKP+
and RMCP+ protocols was very useful in debugging LAN issues. He was able to provide back-up
coverage for the build and BVT engineers, and continued to help with NTE debug.
o Great Place to Work: In working areas of particular interest to him, Jason was fully engaged
and followed through in completing his tasks. One such area was in the debugging of NET, Build,
BVT, SOL and LAN defects; Jason often provided “user friendly” step by step directions for tasks,
using screen-shots to ensure clarity. This type of initiative shows Jason’s natural instinct to step
in and help his team mates.
Evaluation: Areas for Development and/or Improvement
o Results Orientation: Jason needs to clearly understand expectations and work accordingly.
Jason wants more responsibilities and recognition but he has not produced the expected results.
Feedback from team-members suggests that Jason takes longer than expected to complete
tasks, and he gets distracted easily. This led to tasks being reassigned to other team members in
order to maintain the tight schedule. Jason did not keep his lead informed when he was falling
behind, and had to be monitored closely. Toward the end of the year, he was asked to provide
daily status as a remedy and he followed through as requested and provided daily status
updates. Jason should continue to improve in this area by discussing what is expected of him and
ensuring that his plans reflect those expectations.
o Discipline: At times, Jason has been erratic and unreliable, which makes it difficult to plan and
assign him critical tasks, even in his areas of expertise. Jason also did not appear committed to
the project, as evidenced by his disinterest in taking and completing tasks when the team was
strained during the year. Jason was not consistent in his work hours, in attending meetings and
did not communicate in advance with the team about his whereabouts. After considerable
mentoring in this area by senior members of the team, noticeable improvement was seen toward
the end of the year. Jason started attending meetings regularly, followed through on AR’s, and
provided email updates on his task status. Jason should continue to improve by understanding
the importance of this key Intel value, and embracing it in an uncompromising fashion.
o Disagree and Commit: Jason can be passionate regarding his work, and normally this attribute
can help improve the team. However, Jason was perceived to be obsessive about a particular
design or method; at times, he would not let it go if the team or an individual did not agree with
his views. This was most evident in discussions about the scrum process and how it was being
practiced by the team. While the team was trying to agree on a common process, Jason was
quite adamant about how it should be, even when other team members did not agree. Similar
observations were made during the technical discussions as well. Jason should listen to
stakeholder view points and cooperatively evaluate the trade-offs to make the decisions.
Performance Summary
o Based on his performance during the last year, Jason has marginally met the expectations of his
management and is rated as Successful for 2010.
In his new group, Jason should proactively measure his progress against expectations with his
manager, and continue to improve in the identified areas of improvement in order to have a
successful 2011.

focal_gems.summary: Software Engineer (2011): Intel ® Platform Debug Toolkit development: Jason ramped himself on C#, VISA, PDT & DAL architecture in Q1. Jason worked with the VISA architect and design engineers to understand the VISA technology and researched existing tools to find the most appropriate way to add VISA support to the PDT.
focal_gems.evidence:
Intel ® Platform Debug Toolkit development: Jason ramped himself on C#, VISA, PDT & DAL architecture in Q1.  Jason worked with the VISA architect and design engineers to understand the VISA technology and researched existing tools to find the most appropriate way to add VISA support to the PDT.  A legacy “Dfx Lakemore Panel” tool was identified and Jason used the Lakemore Dfx plug-in framework to create a “VISA Panel” with DAL support for the PDT.
VISA customer support:  Jason focused on an initial "light integration" model so that early emulator testing could be performed to identify any critical bugs before the X0 power-on.  During X0 and A0 power-on, Jason supported the VISA Panel in the lab and became a contact for VISA. He maintained a presence in the power on lab to support daily VISA debug activities. He captured customer issues, filed HSDs and took ownership of bugs to ensure a quick turnaround. Jason identified and removed non-critical tasks and learned new skills as needed.  He became an expert on xml style sheets in order to automate several time-consuming conversion tasks.  Jason removed maintenance redundancies by refactoring the VISA-DAL register converter to use a lower level builder.  Jason worked with an engineer to resolve compatibility issues between code bases by moving the VISA panel solution from a software fork to a more maintainable collection of stable libraries.
Trace decoration & OEM VISA:  In Q2, Jason coordinated with the trace decoder team and a DAL hooks expert to add VISA decoration capability to online traces.  He provided input on the design as the same functionality was needed in an OEM version of VISA.  Jason cross trained a co-worker on VISA/DAL development in late Q3 and guided the engineer during development of the OEM version in Q4.

He was responsible for development for VISA (Visualization of Internal Signals Architecture) for the Haswell-Client program. In late Q4, Jason took on another responsibility to monitor an engineer to develop an OEM version of the VISA.


Key Accomplishments
Intel ® Platform Debug Toolkit development: Jason ramped himself on C#, VISA, PDT & DAL architecture in Q1.  Jason worked with the VISA architect and design engineers to understand the VISA technology and researched existing tools to find the most appropriate way to add VISA support to the PDT.  A legacy “Dfx Lakemore Panel” tool was identified and Jason used the Lakemore Dfx plug-in framework to create a “VISA Panel” with DAL support for the PDT.
VISA customer support:  Jason focused on an initial "light integration" model so that early emulator testing could be performed to identify any critical bugs before the X0 power-on.  During X0 and A0 power-on, Jason supported the VISA Panel in the lab and became a contact for VISA. He maintained a presence in the power on lab to support daily VISA debug activities. He captured customer issues, filed HSDs and took ownership of bugs to ensure a quick turnaround. Jason identified and removed non-critical tasks and learned new skills as needed.  He became an expert on xml style sheets in order to automate several time-consuming conversion tasks. He provided input on the design as the same functionality was needed in an OEM version of VISA.  Jason cross trained a co-worker on VISA/DAL development in late Q3 and guided the engineer during development of the OEM version in Q4.

Evaluation: Strengths 
GPTW/Team work: Jason thinks about the other people he works with.  He is considerate of others and recognizes their input, thanking them and including them in conversations.  He is always open for discussion and makes it a point to talk with the team and on 1:1’s.  Jason is consistent and dependable.  He is on time to meetings and traveled to meet with the team every Monday.
SW development process:  Jason is enthusiastic about software development practices, process and used his knowledge to help other team members with development.  He participated in all SCRUM meetings: including demos, code reviews, planning, feedback, and the daily standup.  Jason is familiar with the tools such as SVN, VersionOne, and became an early adopter of code collaborator for code reviews. 
Quality:  Jason strives to continuously learn and improve.  He questioned old design decisions and improved software he and others had made. Jason attended all code review sessions and participated heavily to provide feedback and shown good efforts to review his code.  
 
Evaluation: Areas for Development and/or Improvement
Customer Engagement:  With Jason should be proactive in customer engagement, actively helping in the lab 1-2 times a day in order to understand all VISA related issues.  He should help the PDT team to engage customers using Intel ® PDT in the OR lab and bring issues back to the PDT development team.  Jason should engage with the DAL & customer issues, driving HSDs that block VISA through the entire life cycle to ensure that there are no surprises when customers are asked for feedback on VISA.  All VISA related issues will be noticed to VTG development team/program manager before customer escalating to senior management. 
Become a domain export on VISA architecture:  To develop a better VISA solution to meet all Intel silicon roadmap, Jason needs to improve the VISA micro architectural knowledge and develop a plan to be the VISA experts in VTG. Jason should schedule regular 1:1’s with key VISA architect(s) to learn the micro architecture knowledge in VISA.  Also, he should also have regular meetings with the lakemore panel VISA development team to learn their experiences on VISA. Jason should design a better VISA tool usage by working with VISA debug engineers, Lakemore, DTS development teams to fully integrate VISA tool into the PDT. Jason must insert himself to be the key contact person on the VISA solution for the PDT and gain respect from VISA SV debug teams. 

Performance Summary
Jason’s main contribution in this assessment year was VISA development for PDT. He completed the VISA development as per the plan for HSW-C.  He also provided some mentoring to a new engineer to ramp on VISA OEM support. Keeping his contributions in mind, Jason is being rated SUCCESSFUL for the assessment year 2012.

Review Period Jan 2012 - Dec 2012  Job Title Software Engineer Grade 05  Job Description:
Jason worked as software developer in the Intel ® Platform debug Toolkit and was responsible for development for VISA (Visualization of Internal Signals Architecture) for the Haswell-Client and Haswell-Server program.

Key Accomplishments
VISA plug-in Topology Support: Jason used the topology services in the PDT Framework to eliminate the need for users to select a platform project during VISA panel startup. Jason added Python Scripts Service in the PDT VISA panel, developed the "MCI setup script" for Graphical Trace and expanded the support to the Online E-DRAM Trace. Orange VISA (PCIe-LTSSM-DMI) Solution: In late Q4, Jason discovered there was not enough patch space in the HSW-C & CRW C0 production patch to fit in the LTSSM capabilities. Jason performed a series of experiments and identified some duplicated register programming that can be removed to reduce the size of the VCU patch. Release and customer support: Jason created and maintained register definitions and Hooks per program.  He developed the DAL Hooks for signal decoration in decode, and visa TAP registers for routing visa signals to NOA pins for logic analyzer use. Jason drove for DAL support of BDW GT registers, recognized the need for GT DFT_RING support in the DAL, and identified key owners for implementation.  Jason also provided register definitions used by OA API, allowing the PDT Visa panel to use OA counters in the interview tab.  In addition to release supports, Jason captured customer issues, filed HSDs, took ownership of bugs, and actively tracked HSD to completion to ensure a quick turnaround. There were 0 Emergency and 2 high HSDs against VISA plugs-in by the end of 2012. In late Q4, Jason covered a key VISA engineer for Crystalwell and Haswell Post-Si VISA Tools. IMPACT: Jason ensured an end-to-end VISA solution during releases and PowerOns. His development works also gained Jason a trust from a key VISA pre-silicon engineer to cover him for a month. 

Evaluation: Strengths 
GPTW/Team work: Jason is an active listener.  He is considerate of others and recognizes their input, thanking them and including them in conversations.  He is always open for discussion and makes it a point to talk with the team and on 1:1’s.  
SW development process:  Jason is enthusiastic about software development practices, process and used his knowledge to help other team members with development.  He participated in all SCRUM meetings: including demos, code reviews, planning, feedback, and the daily standup.  Jason is familiar with the tools such as SVN, VersionOne, and became an early adopter of code collaborator for code reviews. 
Quality:  Jason strives to continuously learn and improve.  He questioned old design decisions and improved software he and others had made. Jason attended all code review sessions and participated heavily to provide feedback and shown good efforts to review his code.  
 
Evaluation: Areas for Development and/or Improvement
Become a domain export on VISA architecture:  Jason needs to improve the VISA micro architectural knowledge and develop a plan to be the VISA experts in VTG. Feedback includes: “Assuming Jason will be the contact on Visa, he should improve on his Visa Knowledge”, “I really want Jason to provide clear explanations on VISA architecture”. Jason should schedule regular 1:1’s with key VISA architect(s) to learn the micro architecture.  Also, he should have regular meetings with the lakemore panel VISA development team to learn their experiences on VISA (especially on SoC). Jason needs to bring the knowledge back to the team by chairing technical review sessions for the PDT development teams and other VTG development teams.
Scrum master: As a scrum master of the DP PDT team, Jason is expected to exercise scrum flawlessly in the following areas:
Jason will or must be a team player in facilitating others’ success as their own. Jason must also be comfortable surrendering control to the Product Owner and team.

Review Period Jan 2013 - Dec 2013  Job Title Software Engineer Grade 5  
JOB DESCRIPTION
 
Jason was a software developer on the PDT Trace team.  His responsibilities included new feature design and development, bug fixing, maintenance and support of the PDT Trace software with focus on the VISA GUI panel.
 
KEY ACCOMPLISHMENTS
 
SKL VISA:  Jason ensured VISA was ready for SKL power-on.  He discovered issues in the SKL VISA APIs, and then traveled to IDC to collaborate with the SKL team on a solution and support emulation power-on.  He worked with SKL design and the SKL emulation owner to fix  bugs and cover a pre-silicon test gap with VISA Legacy Channel found in emulation.  All issues were resolved, and VISA exited SKL emulation power on ready for silicon power on.
 
VISA on BDW and GTPO:  Jason moved GTPO functionality from the PDT Advanced Trace Configuration (AdvTC) panel to the VISA panel.  The SKL program would not use the AdvTC panel, but still wanted to use GTPO, so Jason identified a good fit for GTPO programming as part of VISA. Jason then collaborated with the BDW and SKL GT expert to move the functionality, with Jason providing the expertise on PDT VISA panel to correctly integrate the GTPO functionality.  As a result, GTPO was available in the ITP II PDT for SKL and other programs which do not use the Advanced Trace Configuration panel but which do use VISA.
 
BDX VISA enabling:  Jason enabled VISA for the BDX-DE program.  He received the request from the BDX SV team, integrated and validated the collateral, and made the release.  Jason enabled BDX VISA support in ITP II on a short runway in time for silicon power on.

EVALUATION: STRENGTHS
 
Team player: Jason is a strong team player.  Jason volunteered to be the scrum master for his scrum team and performed this duty for the entire year.  Jason introduced demo and retrospective meetings to the team this year.  Sprint demos educate the entire team on what each member is doing, and they celebrate the accomplishment of completing features and reaching objectives.  Retrospectives allow the team the regular opportunity to fix bad behaviors or broken process and to document and repeat BKMs.  360 feedback: "Jason is the scrum master of the PDT team … he has volunteered to do this for the whole 2013 even though he’s been busy w/ his VISA work." "As part of his scrum master roles I saw him address and resolve blocks for fellow teammates."
 
Do the right things right: Jason works to fix bugs once and for all at the source.  He recognizes the inefficiency in repeatedly fixing the same bugs in multiple instances of VISA collateral, so he collaborates with program VISA owners to fix issues at the point in the process where they occur.  360 feedback: "I appreciate Jason’s support for the use of automation whenever feasible; he, like me, dislikes having to manually tweak the final revision of an XML file (for example) just because of some sort of bug in the XML generation process."
 
Continuously develop: The VISA capability continues to evolve as it is used by generation after generation of silicon.  Jason learns what is new in each generation and modifies ITP II VISA support accordingly.  Jason's efforts result in VISA consistently ready for PO.  360 feedback: "Jason is one of the few engineers in VTG who knows about VISA."
 
EVALUATION: DEVELOPMENT AREAS
 
SVE 1.0 Agent of Change: As a company we are at an inflection point.  Intel needs to transform to compete effectively and maintain leadership in this ever-changing world and global economy.  Our SVE 1.0 Transformation goals of decreasing TTM and increasing product output are the results that this transformation must achieve.  We believe that we have the best and brightest people in the industry and we count on you to role model the behaviors that will affect the needed change and to adopt the practices that will yield the desired results.  You are encouraged to be a visible agent of change every day as you work towards our TTM and throughput goals.  As important as delivering on our project commitments are the initiatives of radically increasing commonality, eliminating waste, and proactively partnering across key organizations and stakeholders.  Our key organizational values and practices – a open communication, empowering decision making, informing decisions broadly, progress over perfection, ensuring trust, reuse, sharing ownership, facing reality with courage and being a part of the change – are the means to meet our commitments while forwarding our initiatives.  To quote Intel founder Robert Noyce, “Go off and do something wonderful.”
 
DSD collaboration: Jason should broaden his knowledge of his teammates in DSD, the team areas of expertise, and the solutions the team provides.  He should have 1:1s with technical leaders of other pillars to broaden and deepen his expertise in the Debug Solutions problem space.  By building connections within the organization he can facilitate impediment clearing for his scrum team and recognize opportunities for collaboration and thus increase his scope and impact.
 
Educate the team on VISA: VISA continues to be used in new silicon, and Jason is the DSD VISA expert.  Jason should educate his teammates on VISA.  He should continue to present in scrum team demo sessions and involve team members in code reviews and design sessions. Jason should hold a brown bag session to provide a VISA overview.  By training others on VISA, Jason can secure backup VISA support and accomplish more by working through others.

Performance Summary

For his contributions including ownership of the PDT VISA panel, Jason is rated Successful.  Thank you, Jason!

Job Title:    System Validation Engineer    Review Period:    January, 2014 to December, 2014

Job Description
Jason was responsible for enabling integration and functional tests that cover use cases.  He was responsible for submitting and assisting in triage of defects found through his test development and test execution as well as verifying fixes for these defects.  Jason contributed to communicating the completeness of the Open-IPC-API and NPK features at the release milestones including test coverage, existing gaps, known issues, and assured that the release notes accurately reflect the status of the release.

Key Accomplishments
Skylake VISA/GTPO Support: Early in 2014, Jason transitioned to DSD Validation team but continued to support the PDT throughout the year with projects for various SKL VISA stepping.  These included SKL ULT B0, ULT C0 and SKL M0, Q0, P0.  He was the go to person for triaging PDT VISA Panel bugs. For example, he fixed and helped guide the triage of several SKL PDT bugs (a total of 14 Emergency and 22 High bugs).  Jason also helped deliver the SKL GTPO features to the PDT through mentoring and code reviews.  Impact: The PDT continues to support SKL VISA and GTPO.

NPK Tools validation team: In March, Jason switched over to the Debug Tools Validation team.  He began ramping up on the Open-IPC-API and NPK SDK code and their interfaces with other components in the BXT Post Si debug tool stack (PythonSv, LTB).  He used this knowledge to help debug 39 submitted defects found through his test development and test execution as well as verify fixes for these defects.  Early on, Jason found several important OpenIPC compatibility issues with NPK SDK initialization including: IPC dll loading, 64 bit compatibility, IPC Connect, Jtag API changes.  Jason recognized a gap in communication and scheduled joint Customer/OpenIPC/NPK SDK meetings to encourage developer communication.  Impact: The NPK SDK was able to transition to the OpenIPC tool stack smoothly.

FPGA Setup & NPK SDK Training: Jason took the initiative to quickly ramp up on setup and use of the Xilinx FPGA and became a resident expert with its use with the NPK SDK tools.  He requested materials for, set up, and maintained 4 of the 5 BXT NPK FPGA tests environments known to exist.  He captured this knowledge in an FPGA wiki and used it to train others for use in GUI validation at another site.  He was one of the first to become familiar with the 'new GUI' and trained users in the use of the NPK SDK tools for validation in the simulation environment.  His working test environment allowed him to quickly do a full stack demo of NPK Tools trace capture.  This was done for several groups for BXT PO as well as a video for further training needs.  He received an SRA for getting the BXT FPGA test environment setup.  Impact: NPK SDK Customers have relevant training and training materials.

Release and Integration testing: Jason identified tests gaps and developed an automated test plan. With his experience with the FPGA environment and NPK SDK development Jason identified several key tests covering: initialization, full stack, performance, full trace, trigger, and extract, through TAP and probe mode that were available in the NPK SDK 'google test' environment but were not currently available to automation.  He started the set up of two integration tests hosts on TeamCity and verified they were compatible with the 'google test' environment. Recognition: "Jason caught an issue in the 1450 Debug Tool Stack that broke a previously working NPK use case.   Submitted the defect and notified the involved parties so it could be quickly addressed."  

Strengths
Collaboration: Jason was helpful in supporting the BXT program by using the FPGA environment to quickly test BXT features prior to power on. In this collaboration effort, Jason worked on python scripts to configure VISA trace, a python test to validate trace to memory, and a fully functional script to validate PTI trace.  With the PTI feature in particular, Jason was able to verify the LTB stack was working, discovered nibble order silicon implementation bug, verified the LTB workaround, verified the OpenIPC interface port service, and engaged NPK PTI trace decode developers with software issues well before they would have been discovered during power on.

VISA technical Knowledge: Jason is considered a content expert for VISA and was the go to engineer to address and close several key defects.  His effort with VISA on the SKL client programs have been recognized by his peers and end customers.

Customer Orientation: Jason Agreed to continue to own VISA for SKL client after transitioning to a new role as a Validation System Engineer.  He was very helpful and accommodating in resolving VISA customer’s issues and was timely in responding to customers.  

Improvement/Development Areas
As part of the Integration Validation team the primary objective for Jason this year was to develop and implement automated regression tests that can be used to verify the integration of the NPK software with the rest of the debug tool stack.  Although Jason did a lot of work testing NPK software, and found a number of bugs he still hasn’t delivered on setting up regression tests that verify the integration of the NPK software and the rest of the debug tool stack.  This was and still is a critical deliverable that would allow us to quickly verify new releases of NPK.  Jason needs to partner with the DSD validation engineers in GDC to generate new NPK test cases and continue to work on automating these test cases in TeamCity.  Showing meaningful progress in this area is a must for Jason to be successful this upcoming year.
Communication: Jason received mixed 360 feedbacks in the area of communication. Some co-workers stated that he is clear in his communication, but others have noted difficulty communicating with Jason. Examples provided are Jason e-mails and some of the bugs that he has written are cryptic making it difficult to understand what he is trying to communicate.  Jason should consider the frame of reference of his audience and provide more contexts when he starts a conversation, sends an e-mail or writes a defect.
Jason had communicated an interest to cross train with DSD DCI team as part of his development plan.  His manager discussed Jason’s interest to the DCI team manager and other team leads and came up with a plan for Jason to work 50% of his time for a period of one quarter with the DCI team.  This was a good opportunity for Jason to increase his knowledge in this area and help a team that was in need for his support.  Jason made minimum effort to follow up with this plan and completely missed on this opportunity.
SVE 1.0 Change Agent:  During 2014, SVE achieved great success with our transformative actions; achieving our Scalability goal and making significant progress toward our TTM goals that altogether will increase Intel’s competitive position.  We have to continue this transformation focus into 2015 while we deliver quality products quickly for Intel.  The success we have enjoyed has come through employees seeking to realize and implement the vision in their everyday work.  Everybody plays a part; in 2015, we ask you to embrace and embody our key organizational values and most importantly become a LEADER for change in your role.     

Performance Summary with Rating
Jason started his new role where he contributed to the validation of the Open-IPC-API and NPK and their interfaces with other components in the BXT Post Si debug tool stack (PythonSv, LTB).  He was responsible for enabling Open-IPC-API and NPK unit tests created by development into the build and regression environment.  Working with development to identify and fill any testing gaps as appropriate. 

For 2014 Jason has been rated Successful.  Thank you for your work this year!

Job Title:    Validation Engineer    Review Period:    1/1/2015 to 12/31/2015

Job Description
Jason was a validation engineer in DSD.  During the evaluation period Jason was responsible for ensuring the health of DSD trace debug tools such as the PVT debug stack, and PDT VISA capabilities.  He was responsible for communicating the capability and release quality of the BXT tools being released to OEMs.  

Key Accomplishments
PDT VISA:  Jason continued with his commitment to support the Skylake PDT VISA plugins.  In addition to Skylake, Jason acted as an expert developer and consultant for Broadwell, Brystalwell, Kabylake, CannonLake, and the graphics GTPO trace capabilities.  This resulted in 9+ new projects and a solid GTPO debug capability for each architecture.  Jason ran several training sessions at the request of the trace debug development team, in order to facilitate training and bridge the knowledge gap.  The team requested updated training material to complement the legacy videos and training material.  Jason pooled his knowledge into a "PDT VISA Panel Project Maintenance" document.  This allowed Jason to successfully transition development work to the new team, and by mid-December, the trace debug team made their first project: KBL A0.  Impact: Years after development, PDT Visa continues to be a viable and well used feature.

BXT Support:  Jason was part of a team that worked on regressions to test functionality of Northpeak debug tools for Broxton Power-On. These regressions stressed Northpeak GUI, Python command line and connectivity with OpenIPC. The effort resulted in a significant number of software bugs exposed and early and proactive resolution of these issues. Jason was able to confirm that the NPK, PTI, and Visa use cases he used for the FPGA were still working on an actual BXT platform with very minor changes to his tests.  Jason then extend the tests with automated pass/fail conditions for use in PVT validation.

OEM PVT Validation:  Jason quickly became an expert in the use of the OEM PVT and uncovered several flawed assumptions that would have been dead on arrival. Jason communicated the Orange PVT health and release readiness in status meetings.  Jason brought to light several design architecture assumptions integration difficulties.  One in particular was OpenIPC configuration. Without any intervention a customer visible critical error was POR.  Jason’s drive to address this issue resulted in a cross team push, while not completely solved, many mitigations exist, and both the Installer and GUI now prompt the user for this information.  On LTB issues: "Thanks Jason!  Good to hear LTB fixed the two big issues."  Impact: The OEM PVT health has been brought from obscurity to the main stage and continues to improve with each release.

Early boot trace debug & development:  During BXT Power-On and OEM PVT testing, Jason identified the need for a boot halt script that would work without PythonSV.  Jason assisted in the debug and development of this script with other engineers which was later published with the OEM PVT.  He then took ownership of this area and adapted the OEM boot script for BSSB.  After the process became stable enough, it became apparent that BIOS was not ready for early boot trace.  Jason pushed the BIOS team to support early boot and work with the NPK software POR.  Other features followed including power state management and workarounds that could not be fixed in other areas of the software. Jason is now moving his knowledge back into Red PVT.  Between the boot script, BSSB fixes and workarounds, and BIOS requests, 75% the OEM PVT use cases would not be viable without Jason’s involvement.  Impact: All components involved in BXT trace are now working together to allow early boot trace, the most useful feature in the OEM PVT.

Strengths
Great Place to Work:  Jason is a team player, During BXT power-on, a limited number of target systems were available.  Jason was able to provide FPGA systems in order to debug and reproduce several BXT PO blocking PTI trace issues.  When more targets became available, he worked in the lab to set up Broxton systems for remote team use in other GEOs. Under the guidance of other engineers, Jason trained those in the lab in the use of the NPK tools, triaged defects, and communicated software issues to developers.
Training:  Jason had several opportunities to extend his knowledge to others (PVT tools, PVT testing, OEM PVT testing, VISA maintenance) through training, mentorship, and documentation. In preparation for his sabbatical, Jason quickly ramped up an Application Engineer in the validation of the PVT.  Jason worked with another engineer to open several feature requests (PERs) Product Enhancement Requests, focusing on better error reporting and minimizing the effort of a typical user. 
Quality, System Debug, & Customer Orientation:  A big part of ensuring the quality of software falls on the ability of QA to detect and quickly report problems as soon as they are introduced.  Jason submitted 44 HSDs (as of 8/12 pre-transition to HSD-ES).  Before writing each HSD, Jason takes the effort to investigate, discuss, root cause, and propose solutions to the problem.  When appropriate, the HSD he writes contain workarounds and specific examples.  

Improvement/Development Areas
Embrace change and challenge the Status Quo – Jason has transitioned to a new role in Pre-silicon Platform Architecture. He will need to develop his skills in the areas of HW/SW design and co-verification. Specifically, computer architecture; IA architecture and SoC; advanced C++ and Python; virtual prototyping; and kernel debug. He can start by taking available training from Intel Learning which can help in development and working with his PPA VP team to provide the training on virtual prototyping. 
NPK integration testing – Jason did not deliver the automated regression testing for NPK in TeamCity as part of continuous integration. Although Jason did a lot of work testing NPK software, and found a number of bugs he still hasn’t delivered on setting up regression tests that verify the integration of the NPK software and the rest of the debug tool stack.  This was and still is a critical deliverable that would allow the Validation team to quickly verify new releases of NPK.  
Transition Change Agent - As our MDO and SVE merger was announced, both teams were recognized with the Intel Quality Award (IQA), Intel’s highest organizational award for excellence.  Both organizations received this recognition for achieving bold goals and for driving change, all while putting the customer and Intel first.  Building on this strong foundation, and inspiring even greater contributions as one merged organization will continue to be the life-blood of our combined team where we will be Intel’s voice of quality. Each and every employee plays a role in realizing the success of Intel is achieved by implementing our goals and values into our everyday work.  In 2016, we ask you to embrace and embody the opportunity of the new organization and, most importantly, become a LEADER for change.  

Performance Summary with Rating
Jason has been rated successful for 2015.  Good luck Jason with your new assignment in Pre-silicon Platform Architecture and thank you for all your support to DSD over the years.
